requirements.requirement: Provide an encrypted volume on node1 (LUKS-encrypted block device with a filesystem)
requirements.summary: A LUKS2 volume was created on a 2G loopback-backed image (/dev/loop10), formatted with cryptsetup luksFormat, and given an xfs filesystem. luksDump output confirms LUKS2 with aes-xts-plain64 cipher, and cryptsetup status post-reboot confirms the mapping is active and in use.
Both pre-restart and post-restart evidence show /dev/mapper/secure mounted at /srv/secure as xfs, rw, with df confirming a 2.0G filesystem in use.

requirements.requirement: Volume unlocks and mounts on its own at boot without manual intervention
requirements.summary: A full disruption/recovery cycle was directly observed: pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 33b0e84c... with the volume healthy and mounted (cmd-97438d89878e4ee5); a reboot was triggered and acknowledged (cmd-60c54613f4e94219); the node became unreachable and then returned with a new boot_id 5bf15ff6... (cmd-d611b198a9444cf3, cmd-6032426a982d4bd6, cmd-dfd466b1b65c4917); post-restart evidence shows secure-loop.service and systemd-cryptsetup@secure.service both 'active (exited) since' the new boot time, the LUKS mapping active, /srv/secure mounted rw, the pre-reboot marker file intact, and a new post-reboot write succeeding, all without any manual command performing the unlock/mount (cmd-14a2bac983a64a7c). Persistence of crypttab/fstab/enabled unit was reconfirmed post-reboot (cmd-70982111c8344a70).

requirements.requirement: Auto-unlock mechanism does not expose the key insecurely
requirements.summary: The LUKS keyfile is generated with 2048 bits of random data, stored at /etc/luks/secure.key with mode 400 owned by root:root, verified both immediately after creation and after reboot.

overall_summary: The task's material outcome — an encrypted (LUKS2) volume mounted at /srv/secure on node1 that auto-unlocks and auto-mounts at boot — is directly and coherently demonstrated through a genuine reboot cycle: healthy pre-restart baseline, a real boot-id change confirming the node actually rebooted, and post-restart state showing the loop device reattached, LUKS volume unlocked, filesystem mounted, and prior data intact, all without manual intervention. The main deduction is operational hygiene: the executor left an unauthenticated temporary yum repo enabled and left several backup/log files behind without evident cleanup.
limitations: No evidence was captured of whether /etc/yum.repos.d/vault-temp.repo, /etc/crypttab.bak, /etc/fstab.bak, or the /tmp/yum*.log files were ever removed after task completion — only their creation and their presence in the after-executor snapshot are visible.
Only a single restart cycle is captured; long-term boot reliability across multiple reboots cannot be confirmed from this evidence alone.

The provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol appears to coincide with (or be satisfied by) the same reboot performed for the task's own auto-mount verification; no separate/independent restart evidence trace was provided, though the single captured cycle covers boot-identity change, pre/post health, and recovered state for the one managed node.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most mutations were necessary and appropriately scoped (loopback image, keyfile, LUKS format, systemd unit, crypttab/fstab entries), and the destructive discovery command sequences (STEP 1-2 partial failures) were harmless dry runs corrected in the next command. However, the executor added a temporary, unauthenticated third-party yum repo (/etc/yum.repos.d/vault-temp.repo, gpgcheck=0, cmd-2fdb49152acd44db) to work around missing RHEL subscription access, and left it enabled on the system with no evidence it was removed after cryptsetup installation completed — this is a retained, security-relevant residue (an unauthenticated package source persists on a production-facing RHEL box). Backup files /etc/crypttab.bak and /etc/fstab.bak (created in cmd-d3693acf1bd34c2e) and stray /tmp/yum.log, /tmp/yumclean.log, /tmp/yuminstall.log (visible in the after-executor temp-files snapshot) were also left behind; these are low-severity but unnecessary residue with no evidence of cleanup.
